chapters.question_prompt: How do you structure a lean 1 FT + 3 C (4 people) -> 2 FT + 4 C (6 people) pod, enforce weekly scorecards, and build transferable books that command a premium exit multiple (or durable cash cow)?
chapters.title: Pod Architecture, Contractor KPIs & Exit Valuation
chapters.subtitle: Parcel-Level Accountability, QGIS Evidence, Title-Insured Closings, Accrual Cohorts & Transferable Rights Under 17 U.S.C. Section 204(a)
chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #6, Land Flipping, ranks #15 with a 86/100 Money-to-Manpower Score. Build around six chapter-mapped execution plays: off-market sourcing, GIS screening, comparable-led offers, title/access diligence, minor subdivisions, and title-insured dispositions. The lean pod uses one full-time principal and three contractors; the scaled pod adds an operations manager and a subdivision specialist. Canonical annual owner net profit is $24,000 Conservative, $157,250 Base, and $375,000 Scaled, on gross parcel sale proceeds rather than intermediary fees. Transferability comes from documented access, closed-loop contractor QA, parcel-level accrual books, assigned work-product rights, and counterparty exposure capped at 25%. Value repeatable earnings separately from surplus land, and price replacement labor before treating the business as a durable cash cow.

sections.heading: 1. Assign six execution plays without disguising a large team
paragraphs: Start with four dedicated people, not four departments. The full-time principal owns capital allocation, offer authority, exceptions, and final disposition pricing. Contractor one handles off-market sourcing, GIS screening, and comparable-led offer preparation as a parcel-intelligence seat. Contractor two coordinates title/access diligence, assembling recorded instruments and tracking curative work without substituting personal conclusions for title counsel or a licensed surveyor. Contractor three owns listing production, buyer follow-up, and closing coordination for title-insured dispositions, subject to the applicable brokerage rules. Minor subdivisions remain a principal-led exception play until volume supports specialist capacity. These are the six chapter-mapped plays; each parcel receives a primary play tag and may carry secondary tags without being counted twice in throughput. Airtable can hold the operating register, QGIS the spatial evidence, and a controlled document repository the closing record. Outside title insurers, attorneys, surveyors, and escrow providers are transaction vendors rather than hidden dedicated pod seats. Their invoices still enter parcel economics. Publish an authority map distinguishing who prepares, who checks, who signs, and who releases funds. No contractor may turn a promising screenshot into a binding acquisition commitment. Record an alternate reviewer so a principal's absence does not silently suspend diligence.

Buy defined deliverables rather than vague availability. An illustrative Base contractor budget is $1,250 monthly for parcel intelligence, $1,500 for diligence coordination, and $1,750 for disposition coordination: $54,000 annually before separately scoped transaction services. Those amounts are planning assumptions inside existing scenario costs, not additions to canonical profit. Specify capacity, complexity limits, accepted evidence, and revision obligations before requesting bids. For example, require a first parcel screen within two business days after complete inputs, a title-exception log within three business days after receipt of the commitment, and a closing checklist within one business day after escrow opens. Missing county records pause the relevant clock only when the contractor logs the dependency and next follow-up date. Pay fixed scope fees against accepted batches; reserve any closing-related compensation for arrangements permitted by applicable licensing rules. Reject per-offer bonuses that encourage weak access assumptions or artificially generous comparable selection. Rework attributable to an omitted contracted check is included; a newly discovered easement dispute is a separately priced scope change. Have counsel assess worker classification from actual control and economic dependence, not merely the contractor label. Review rates quarterly against accepted output, error cost, and available specialist capacity.

At the scaled configuration, the second full-time seat becomes an operations manager, while the fourth contractor supplies subdivision and entitlement expertise. The resulting six-person pod is two employees and four contractors, not six interchangeable acquisition agents. The manager owns queue discipline, reviewer assignments, monthly close coordination, and vendor service levels; the principal retains investment limits and unusual land-risk decisions. The subdivision specialist coordinates lot-yield assumptions, agency submissions, and licensed technical work within the specialist's actual credentials. Do not imply that a planning consultant can stamp a survey. Add these seats when funded workload and recurring contribution support them, rather than when one unusually profitable parcel closes. Require an eight-week capacity forecast, a thirteen-week cash forecast, and demonstrated completion of the existing team's checklists. Measure principal dependence by tracking substantive interventions per closing and hours needed to resolve exceptions. A buyer will discount a business whose owner alone remembers which road is public or which builder actually pays on time. Document substitute coverage for every recurring task, but keep bank release rights narrow and independently verified. The smaller pod remains valid when deal quality is strong and additional volume would merely increase inventory age or expose the business to unfamiliar jurisdictions.

callout.title: Four habits that preserve specialist leverage
callout.body: Make the evidence portable before increasing parcel throughput or adding another county.
items: Save the county road-maintenance response beside the recorded access instrument; a road appearing on an aerial image proves neither legal access nor public maintenance.
Store comparable deed references and adjustment notes, not just portal links; stale listings and expired subscriptions otherwise erase the offer rationale.
Price survey mobilization and minimum trip charges before choosing a subdivision market; scattered low-value parcels can consume the apparent lot-split spread.
Prepare a backup title contact before the first difficult closing, and preserve the original insurer's unresolved exception history when moving a file.

sections.heading: 2. Run a weekly scorecard that penalizes hidden defects
paragraphs: Run the weekly meeting from a dated snapshot rather than a live dashboard that changes during discussion. Each Monday, freeze parcel stage, committed capital, latest evidence date, next action, and accountable seat. Track the six plays through a shared funnel: sourced, screened, offered, contracted, cleared, acquired, listed, and closed. Count unique parcels for screening and unique purchase agreements for contracting; count child lots separately only after assigning a parent link and allocating basis. Report first-pass QA acceptance as accepted submissions divided by reviewed submissions, and separately show critical defects discovered after acceptance. An initial internal target of 95% first-pass acceptance can guide coaching, but never excuses a single unsupported access claim. SLA attainment uses completed deliverables due that week as its denominator, with overdue open work displayed separately to prevent disappearance from the metric. Show median stage age alongside the oldest file because averages hide stranded land. Follow accepted offers into closed acquisitions by county and outreach cohort, rather than celebrating signatures that collapse during diligence. Finish the meeting with named actions, deadlines, and a capital decision for every exception. The principal should inspect the riskiest changes, not reread every clean parcel screen.

Enforce concentration before exposure is created. Set a maximum of 25% for any related buyer group's share of trailing-twelve-month recognized sale proceeds and a separate 25% limit for its share of contracted receivables. Aggregate affiliates, common guarantors, and entities sharing the same actual decision-maker when evidence supports the relationship. Measure future exposure using the signed closing schedule as well as historical results, since a repeat builder can dominate next quarter without dominating last year. Add a 25% acquisition-cost exposure cap for any seller group or sourcing counterparty across open commitments. During startup, one closing necessarily produces concentrated revenue; disclose that condition, calculate the minimum four independent equal-sized buyer groups needed for a balanced book, and prohibit representing the portfolio as diversified. Pause incremental exposure to an over-limit group while seeking independent buyers or reducing commitments. For critical title, escrow, and survey counterparties, track unsettled cash or committed project cost separately; process four comparable closings sequentially if concurrent exposure would otherwise concentrate. A sole-vendor dependency remains visible even when only one transaction is open. Do not satisfy a cap by splitting invoices among affiliated entities or shrinking the denominator through selective reporting.

Make QA a separate measurement from speed. Sample ordinary screens weekly and review every parcel with access ambiguity, floodway overlap, an environmental history flag, or a subdivision assumption driving the price. A QGIS overlay identifies questions; it does not establish a recorded easement, resolve a boundary, or replace local zoning confirmation. Require the reviewer to cite the controlling instrument or agency response and explain any mismatch with the listing. For environmental concerns, route the acquisition to an environmental professional early enough to assess whether all appropriate inquiries are required for an intended CERCLA defense. Treat 40 CFR Part 312 as a transaction-specific diligence framework, not a universal certificate that makes land harmless. Track defect cost through rework fees, extension payments, survey changes, and lost deposits. Assign the operational cause without promising recovery from a contractor beyond the agreement. When a contractor repeatedly misses evidence standards, narrow the scope, require retraining, or transfer the work; accelerating payment alone will not repair technical judgment. Close each weekly review by comparing forecast closings with actual cash availability, including property taxes and carrying costs on parcels that did not move. A fast funnel with deteriorating inventory age is a warning, not operating leverage.

callout.title: Four pre-flight checks before expanding the pod
callout.body: Release additional workload only after the principal records these checks against current evidence.
items: Verify that each active parcel has a signed purchase file, access evidence, unresolved title exceptions, and an accountable next-action owner.
Verify that funded contractor scopes cover the eight-week queue and that licensed activities are assigned only to appropriately authorized providers.
Verify buyer, seller, receivable, and critical-vendor exposure calculations; identify startup concentration explicitly and stop incremental over-limit exposure.
Verify the thirteen-week cash forecast includes deposits, tax bills, curative work, and slower closings without spending refundable buyer funds.

sections.heading: 3. Build parcel-level accrual books and assign the operating assets
paragraphs: Use parcel-level accrual management books even when a permitted tax method differs. Create a permanent parcel identifier that joins the purchase agreement, settlement statement, bank movement, title policy, and sale record. Carry land held for resale as inventory under the adopted accounting policy; do not expense every acquisition when cash leaves the bank and then describe the later sale as almost pure margin. Record capitalizable acquisition and improvement costs consistently, release the applicable basis when revenue is recognized, and separately track selling costs and period overhead. Have the accountant document the relevant inventory and capitalization treatment, including applicable small-business exceptions under federal tax rules. Gross parcel sale proceeds are the canonical revenue basis here; acquisition outlays belong in costs rather than reducing reported revenue to a brokerage-like fee. Refundable deposits remain liabilities until the contract and accounting facts support another treatment. Seller-held notes require distinct principal, interest, collectibility, and cash collection schedules; receiving a note does not create cash available for another acquisition. Reconcile escrow activity to the ledger instead of assuming a net wire explains every cost. Retain a documented cutoff policy so a December closing cannot migrate between years merely to improve a buyer presentation.

Create acquisition cohorts by quarter, county, and primary play, preserving the original underwriting case beside actual results. For each cohort, show acquired cost, improvement spend, carrying cost, recognized proceeds, realized contribution, remaining inventory basis, and cash recovered. Calculate sold-parcel margin separately from whole-cohort results so profitable early exits do not conceal unsold remnants. For a minor subdivision, allocate parent basis and shared costs using a documented reasonable method, such as relative expected sales values supported at allocation; review the method with the accountant and retain subsequent changes. An illustrative $120,000 allocable project with expected lot values of $80,000 and $120,000 assigns $48,000 and $72,000 of basis, respectively. Those are teaching inputs, not additional canonical revenue. Reconcile every management profit bridge to the annual ledger. Conservative revenue of $200,000 less $176,000 total costs yields $24,000; Base revenue of $850,000 less $692,750 yields $157,250; Scaled revenue of $1,500,000 less $1,125,000 yields $375,000. The respective margins remain 12%, 18.5%, and 25%. Contractor fees, acquisitions, and other costs must fit inside those totals. Separate capital contributions, borrowing, and principal repayments from operating proceeds, and explain any book-to-tax differences without rewriting the operating scorecard.

Treat the operating system as an asset bundle that needs evidence of ownership and usable transfer rights. Obtain signed contractor assignments covering custom screening scripts, original listing copy, photographs, SOPs, and database structures, with clearly identified pre-existing materials and permitted reuse. Under 17 U.S.C. section 204(a), a copyright ownership transfer generally requires a signed writing from the owner or authorized agent; paying an invoice alone does not supply that instrument. A contract cannot assign third-party mapping rights that the contractor never owned. Inventory QGIS project dependencies, county data terms, paid comparable subscriptions, and photography licenses, identifying which assets transfer and which a buyer must license independently. Keep company-controlled administrator accounts, documented access levels, and tested exports without sharing personal credentials. Record assignment and change-of-control provisions in vendor and customer agreements, because a polished data room does not override a counterparty's contractual rights. Preserve parcel evidence with dates and version history so a buyer can reproduce an underwriting decision after the original contractor leaves. At monthly close, export the ledger, inventory register, open commitments, and relationship map to a restricted repository. Test restoration quarterly. Transferable books require both reconciled numbers and a lawful, practical way to keep operating.

sop_steps.action: Export active, acquired, subdivided, and sold parcel identifiers with dated stage histories.
sop_steps.detail: The principal in the lean pod, or operations manager in the scaled pod, resolves duplicate identifiers and retains parent-child links before ledger reconciliation.

sop_steps.title: Reconcile cash, escrow, and basis
sop_steps.action: Match settlement activity to bank entries, inventory movements, deposit liabilities, and parcel costs.
sop_steps.detail: Log unmatched items with an owner and resolution date; keep borrowing and owner contributions outside recognized parcel sale proceeds.

sop_steps.detail: Restrict access to authorized reviewers and test a sample parcel reconstruction using only the archived records rather than the principal's memory.

sections.heading: 4. Underwrite the exit multiple and the cash-cow alternative
paragraphs: Separate the value of an operating engine from the value of land already owned. A small land-flipping shop may attract an asset buyer who wants discounted inventory but pays little for sourcing routines. An owner-operator buyer may instead value transferable seller's discretionary earnings, while a strategic buyer may evaluate earnings after replacing the principal's continuing work. Canonical owner net profit is neither automatically discretionary earnings nor automatically EBITDA. Build a bridge that identifies actual owner compensation, interest, taxes, depreciation, documented exceptional expenses, and required replacement labor, using the accounting definitions agreed for the transaction. Do not add back routine survey bills, recurring marketing, or title-curative work merely because each parcel is different. For planning rather than a claimed market quotation, test 1.5 to 2.5 times verified owner-operated earnings, and 2.0 to 3.0 times earnings after necessary replacement labor for a demonstrably transferable platform. These ranges are sensitivities, not observed comparable transactions. Exceptional access risk, thin records, concentrated buyers, or stale inventory can reduce goodwill to zero. A premium requires evidence that the buyer inherits a repeatable process and enough ongoing capital, rather than a demanding job wrapped around a speculative land portfolio.

Apply the sensitivity only after stating its denominator. If diligence establishes that Base owner net profit of $157,250 equals the agreed owner-operated earnings measure without further adjustments, 1.5 to 2.5 times implies $235,875 to $393,125 for the operating-business value under that stated asset perimeter. If the Scaled $375,000 requires $75,000 of additional annual replacement labor beyond costs already recorded, adjusted earnings become $300,000; 2.0 to 3.0 times implies $600,000 to $900,000. The $75,000 is an illustrative diligence adjustment, not a revision to the canonical scorecard, and must not duplicate the existing operations manager's expense. Specify whether ordinary parcel inventory is included in normalized working capital supporting the quoted value. If it is included, adding the same inventory again overstates consideration. If inventory is excluded, price the parcel schedule separately and show how the buyer funds replacement stock. Reconcile operating value to seller equity proceeds through debt, excess cash, agreed working-capital adjustments, transaction costs, and any holdback. Price genuinely surplus land separately using parcel evidence and disposition costs, rather than assuming its ledger basis equals realizable value. Compare an earnout's collection risk with a lower cash-at-close offer.

Prepare the exit package before deciding to sell. Assemble twenty-four months of reconciled monthly books where available, complete cohort histories, a current parcel inventory schedule, counterparty concentration reports, and a role-level intervention log. A younger business should present its actual operating history rather than manufacturing an annualized track record. Let a prospective buyer sample closed parcels backward from proceeds to acquisition evidence and forward from original cohorts to remaining inventory. Offer controlled document access and redact unnecessary personal information until the transaction justifies fuller disclosure. For a cash-cow strategy, use the same evidence to calculate distributable cash after replacement inventory, debt service, taxes, and a funded downside reserve; accounting profit alone does not establish withdrawal capacity. Re-run the thirteen-week forecast with delayed closings and lower sale prices before making distributions. Keep the principal's required hours visible, because an attractive margin coupled with constant emergency intervention is not passive ownership. Choose sale, hold, or selective inventory liquidation by comparing achievable net proceeds with risk-adjusted future cash and the owner's desired workload. The durable advantage is disciplined parcel selection backed by transferable evidence, not a headline multiple obtained by ignoring how much capital the next acquisition cycle consumes.

chapters.pull_quote: A land business earns a premium when the next owner can reproduce the decisions, reconcile the cash, and close without borrowing the seller's memory.
action_checklist: Assign the six execution plays to the four-person pod, record signing limits, and define the funded workload that justifies the six-person configuration.
Contract for accepted evidence, revision scope, delivery clocks, and permitted compensation; assess classification and licensing against actual duties.
Freeze a weekly scorecard covering QA, overdue work, inventory age, capital commitments, and related-counterparty exposure capped at 25%.
Close parcel-level accrual books monthly and reconcile exactly to $24,000, $157,250, and $375,000 in the three canonical annual owner-profit cases.
Collect signed work-product assignments, verify third-party data rights, and test restoration of the parcel evidence and accounting archive.
Prepare an earnings-normalization bridge, define inventory treatment, and compare attainable sale proceeds with cash available after capital recycling.

chapters.question_prompt: What is the exact Day-1-to-Day-30 execution schedule for launching land flipping, and what quantitative thresholds govern Kill, Fix, or Scale decisions at Day 30/60/90?
chapters.title: The First 30-Day Launch Sprint & Kill / Fix / Scale Gates
chapters.subtitle: A Four-Person Parcel Acquisition Sprint Across QGIS, Recorded Access, Title Commitments, County Plat Rules, and Cash-Controlled Resale
chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #6, Land Flipping, ranks #15 with a 86/100 Money-to-Manpower Score. This chapter maps six operator plays into one controlled launch: GIS discount sourcing, access-verified rural parcels, utility-ready infill, assemblage, minor subdivisions, and title-insured resale. One full-time owner and three contractors build a measurable pipeline without treating a thirty-day sprint as a promised closing. Days 1–30 establish county economics, contact owners, investigate responsive parcels, and authorize only evidence-backed commitments. Day 30/60/90 decisions separate channel failure from fixable diligence delays and earned expansion. Annual owner profit remains $24,000 Conservative, $157,250 Base, and $375,000 Scaled. Gross parcel sale proceeds are revenue; acquisition, carrying, selling, and operating costs remain real deductions. A $6,000 monthly launch ceiling protects capital while parcel evidence accumulates.

key_metrics.label: Conservative
key_metrics.context: Annual gross parcel sale proceeds; acquisition costs included in net margin
key_metrics.note: 12% net margin; $24,000 annual owner net profit; 1 FT + 3 C

key_metrics.context: Annual gross parcel sale proceeds; acquisition costs included in net margin

sections.heading: 1. Days 1–7: Select One County and Establish the Capital Boundary
paragraphs: Start with one county, one parcel-size band, and one buyer use case rather than a statewide mailing list. Candidate #6 rewards disciplined screening, not maximum acreage under contract. For this sprint, map six operator plays explicitly: P1 GIS discount sourcing; P2 access-verified rural parcels; P3 utility-ready infill; P4 adjacent-owner assemblage; P5 minor subdivisions; and P6 title-insured resale. These are this chapter's operating labels, not six separate businesses to launch simultaneously. P1 feeds every opportunity, P6 closes the loop, and the owner selects either P2 or P3 as the initial product. Keep P4 and P5 as documented exceptions until buyer demand and county procedures support their additional complexity. On Day 1, write the intended purchaser, maximum parcel basis, allowed zoning categories, minimum usable area, and excluded conditions into a one-page buy box. On Day 2, examine county recorder documents, assessor exports, local planning rules, FEMA mapping, and actual recorded sales. QGIS organizes overlays; it does not establish boundaries, ownership, or legal access. Reject counties where available evidence cannot support at least ten relevant closed sales from the preceding twelve months without mixing incompatible parcel uses or infrastructure conditions. Record the search boundary so later expansion cannot disguise weak evidence.

Assign the four-person pod before buying data. The full-time owner controls offers, capital allocation, seller conversations, and final underwriting. Contractor one maintains parcel records, QGIS layers, and comparable-sale tracking. Contractor two coordinates title, surveying, access documents, and planning inquiries with qualified local providers. Contractor three handles authorized outreach administration, listing production, and buyer follow-up, using a licensed broker where the activity requires one. Surveyors, laboratories, closing firms, and counsel remain separately purchased services; their invoices must still enter parcel economics and workload reporting. Cap the owner's planned week at forty hours: twelve for sourcing and seller calls, twelve for underwriting, eight for transaction coordination, and eight for buyer development and management. Give each contractor a ten-hour weekly planning allowance during the pilot, subject to actual rates and the spending ceiling. Hours are capacity limits, not evidence that every specialist can be retained at the implied price. Maintain one Airtable or spreadsheet record per assessor parcel number, with a separate county identifier to prevent collisions. Store source dates, document links, responsible person, next action, and cash exposure. Never let an attractive asking price substitute for a complete parcel record or a confirmed person responsible for resolving its outstanding questions.

Set the first month's non-acquisition cash ceiling at $6,000 before outreach starts. Allocate $1,500 to data and outreach, $1,200 to parcel analysis, $1,000 to title and access investigation, $800 to field and planning checks, $900 to buyer development, and $600 to contingency. These are proposed allocations within the volume's $3,000–$15,000 monthly operating range, not vendor quotations. Include contractor invoices inside these buckets rather than adding labor afterward. At the $50,000 startup-capital floor, ring-fence another $18,000 for three future months at the same ceiling. That leaves no more than $26,000 for purchase price, escrow deposits, and parcel-specific closing obligations after the first month's planned spend. Larger acquisitions require more capital or a different buy box; do not consume the operating reserve to force a deal. Treat deposits as committed cash even when refundable, and record their refund deadlines. Review incurred costs plus signed obligations twice weekly. If specialist quotes exceed the budget, reduce parcel count or stop a play before ordering work. The three-to-twelve-month time to first deal makes liquidity preservation more important than producing a ceremonial Day-30 purchase. No debt proceeds or anticipated resale receipts belong in available cash until the funds are actually accessible.

callout.title: Four Checks Before the First Acquisition Commitment
callout.body: An accepted price does not authorize a purchase. The owner records these four checks before releasing acquisition funds or allowing protections to expire.
items: Verify the seller's signing authority and match the legal description across the deed, commitment, contract, and survey evidence.
Obtain documented legal access and inspect the recorded easement scope; a visible road or assessor frontage line is insufficient.
Confirm intended use, utility feasibility, environmental investigation scope, and any required plat action with the responsible local authority or specialist.
Recalculate purchase cash, closing charges, downside proceeds, and remaining operating reserve using written quotes and dated comparable evidence.

sections.heading: 2. Days 8–14: Run One Measured Outreach Cohort and Underwrite Responses
paragraphs: Build a 200-parcel research cohort during Week 2, then remove duplicates, parcels outside the buy box, unresolved ownership conflicts, and obvious disqualifiers. The target is 150 screened records and 100 distinct owners reached through documented delivery, not 200 indiscriminate messages. Prefer individually addressed postal letters for the initial test, with accurate purchaser identity and no suggestion of government affiliation. Calling and texting require a separate review of 47 U.S.C. § 227, applicable state requirements, and suppression procedures; a purchased telephone number does not itself establish permission. Record sent, returned, delivered or reasonably delivery-supported, responded, qualified, and offered as separate events. Use a consistent maturity window: evaluate response rates only after fourteen calendar days from supported delivery. A Day-14 mailing therefore contributes mature observations by Day 28, whereas a replacement mailed on Day 25 does not. Count owners rather than parcels for response rates because one owner may control several lots. Keep undelivered records outside the response denominator and inside the address-quality denominator. Do not mix a rural letter cohort with infill broker referrals when calculating channel performance. Their acquisition costs and conversion paths differ materially, and blending them would conceal which repeatable process deserves the next dollar.

Define a qualified seller conversation before the first response arrives: the person has plausible authority, identifies the parcel, expresses willingness to discuss a sale, and provides a price expectation or agrees to review an offer. A callback requesting removal is not qualified demand. Target five qualified conversations from the first 100 mature delivered contacts, but treat five percent as a pilot decision threshold rather than a market benchmark. For each promising parcel, retrieve at least three genuinely comparable closed transactions and explain differences in access, usable acreage, utility distance, entitlement, and sale timing. Use a conservative resale estimate based on supportable adjustments, not the highest neighboring listing. Calculate maximum purchase price as expected gross proceeds minus closing and selling costs, diligence, carrying costs, allocated overhead, and required profit. As an illustrative Base-margin screen, a $100,000 resale supports $81,500 of total costs and $18,500 of profit. One possible cost stack is $55,000 acquisition, $4,000 diligence, $7,500 settlement and marketing, $5,000 carrying, and $10,000 allocated overhead. That example exceeds the smallest launch's acquisition capacity; it illustrates underwriting, not permission to spend beyond available cash. Quote each material input before converting the screen into a binding commitment.

Separate desktop rejection from paid investigation. P2 requires a recorded access path benefiting the actual parcel, practical entry conditions, and evidence that maintenance obligations are affordable. P3 requires utility-provider information about service availability, connection charges, capacity, and timing; a line on the next street does not establish a usable connection. P4 requires an identified adjacent buyer and a premium supported by their use case, not a speculative assemblage multiplier. P5 requires written procedural guidance about subdivision, frontage, drainage, minimum lot dimensions, and infrastructure obligations. In applicable unincorporated Texas areas, Local Government Code § 232.001 supplies a county plat framework, with exceptions and additional rules requiring local review. Never assume that drawing two polygons creates two saleable lots. P6 requires a closing path that addresses commitment requirements and material exceptions before promising clean delivery. Ask the title company what coverage is actually available; insurance does not automatically establish buildability or remove exclusions. By Day 14, the owner should have three documented offer candidates or a specific diagnosis explaining the shortfall. If every candidate depends on an unpriced easement, rezoning, or utility extension, the county may be workable but the selected product and capital envelope are not aligned.

callout.title: Four Land-Specific Ways to Avoid Paying for False Positives
callout.body: Buy inexpensive evidence first, but never confuse inexpensive evidence with a final professional determination.
items: Ask the recorder for the easement instrument and amendments before commissioning field work; the grant may exclude the intended use or benefit another parcel.
Call the utility's service-design desk with the parcel identifier and intended load; a general customer-service statement rarely prices extension work.
Interview adjacent owners about actual purchase interest before modeling assemblage value, and keep their statements separate from a binding purchase commitment.
Maintain rejected comparable sales alongside accepted ones; a documented exclusion log prevents the next analyst from reintroducing inflated subdivision or improved-property prices.

sections.heading: 3. Days 15–21: Resolve Fatal Defects Before Advancing Contract Exposure
paragraphs: Week 3 turns seller interest into a controlled investigation, not an obligation to rescue every attractive parcel. Issue offers only after the owner signs the underwriting record and checks cash availability. Use locally appropriate contract forms and transaction counsel when drafting or modifying protections. Specify inspection periods, title review rights, deposit handling, permitted assignment if relevant, closing conditions, and the procedure for timely termination. Do not assume a contingency exists because a spreadsheet contains an unresolved issue. Open a deadline register immediately after execution, with reminders five, three, and one business day before each critical notice deadline. Route funds through the selected closing provider and independently verify wiring instructions using a previously established telephone number. A changed email attachment is not sufficient verification. Cap the pilot at two simultaneous paid diligence files; this limits both cash leakage and the coordinator's task load. Each file receives a defect ledger listing the issue, source document, responsible resolver, estimated cost, completion date, and effect on the offer. If a seller will not provide enough investigation time to answer a material question, decline or renegotiate rather than substituting confidence for evidence. The owner's signature records a decision, not merely attendance at a review.

Investigate environmental constraints in proportion to the parcel's history and intended use, with qualified environmental professionals determining appropriate scope. County GIS, EPA mapping, aerial history, and FEMA layers identify questions; they cannot establish absence of contamination, wetlands, or developable area. CERCLA's bona fide prospective purchaser framework includes requirements in 42 U.S.C. § 9601(40) and § 9607(r), while 40 CFR Part 312 governs all appropriate inquiries. Some inquiry components require updating within 180 days before acquisition, and the overall timing framework includes a one-year limit. Have the professional confirm applicable components and continuing obligations rather than treating a report date as a universal shield. Where fill or dredged material may affect jurisdictional waters, examine Clean Water Act § 404, 33 U.S.C. § 1344, before modeling earthwork as routine preparation. For access, distinguish recorded legal rights, physical usability, and lender or title-insurer treatment. For zoning, obtain the permitted-use basis and dimensional constraints from the responsible authority. A parcel can have an insurable ownership interest while remaining commercially unsuitable for the intended purchaser. Record that distinction in the investment memo so a clean title discussion cannot silently replace the separate buildability investigation.

Price the exit while diligence is still reversible. Contractor three develops a buyer evidence sheet with two independent price opinions, three comparable closings, likely buyer financing, estimated marketing time, and disposition expenses. A broker opinion is useful evidence but not a completed sale. When representing others for compensation, check the governing licensing rules; California Business and Professions Code §§ 10130–10131 illustrate why buying for one's own account and performing brokerage for another are distinct activities. Do not assume an ownership structure or assignment label resolves every state's requirements. Build a downside case with resale proceeds ten percent below the supported estimate and an additional six months of quoted carrying costs. The pilot purchase rule requires nonnegative owner profit under that downside and at least an 18.5 percent modeled net margin under the supported case, after allocated overhead. These are selection thresholds, not a restatement of the portfolio's realized outcomes. For example, an extra $3,000 carry on the $100,000 illustration leaves $5,500 profit after a ten percent price reduction. An unpaid easement cure can erase that cushion immediately. Reprice or terminate when verified costs break either threshold; do not preserve a contract merely because diligence money has already been spent.

sections.heading: 4. Days 22–30 and Reviews at 60/90: Earn Expansion with Cohort Evidence
paragraphs: Use the final nine days to finish evidence, inspect workload, and reconcile cash rather than manufacture a closing milestone. Candidate #6 normally needs three to twelve months to reach a first deal, so Day 30 measures process validity and investable pipeline. Reconcile every invoice, refundable deposit, signed purchase obligation, and remaining reserve on Day 24. On Day 25, ask each contractor to report actual hours and unresolved tasks. If the owner exceeds forty planned hours or a contractor exceeds ten for two consecutive weeks, stop expanding file count until work is removed or repriced. On Day 26, audit ten randomly selected parcel records against original sources. Require at least nine complete files, with zero misidentified owners or unsupported legal-access conclusions. On Days 27–29, mature the outreach cohort, refresh the pipeline, and classify defects as fatal, curable within ten business days, or awaiting an external milestone. Day 30 produces a written Kill, Fix, or Scale decision for each channel and play. An immature cohort receives Fix, not a fabricated response rate. A healthy research pipeline can earn more screening capacity while still earning no authority to purchase a parcel.

Apply the decision matrix in order: capital and fatal-defect stops first, qualified evidence second, expansion last. Kill means stop new spending on the affected channel, play, or parcel and preserve contractual rights; it does not mean abandon existing obligations. Fix means hold spending flat, name one bottleneck, and give its owner ten business days to produce a specific correction. Scale means increase screened or contacted volume by no more than twenty-five percent per review while preserving the same purchase rules and reserve. At Day 30, require 100 mature delivered contacts, five qualified seller conversations, three costed offers, and one diligence-ready candidate before expanding sourcing. Diligence-ready means plausible seller agreement on price, complete preliminary underwriting, an identified investigation path, and affordable cash exposure; it is not a title clearance. At Day 60, require 200 mature contacts, ten qualified conversations, six costed offers, and one executed investigation-protected contract. At Day 90, require 300, fifteen, and nine respectively, plus one fully underwritten acquisition-ready file and two evidenced buyer prospects. These cumulative targets test repeatability, not a predicted sales calendar. Failure to close by Day 90 alone does not trigger termination when the milestones, liquidity, and priced investigation path remain intact.

Keep cash-control reporting separate from annual earnings reconciliation. The launch ceiling is $6,000 by Day 30, $12,000 cumulatively by Day 60, and $18,000 by Day 90 for non-acquisition pilot outlays. Purchase principal and closing commitments sit in a separate exposure schedule, never outside total cash control. Categorize direct parcel costs, inventory, and period overhead consistently with the accountant's treatment; deposits and unsold land are not completed-sale proceeds. The canonical Conservative case is $200,000 gross parcel sale proceeds less $176,000 total costs, leaving $24,000 owner profit at twelve percent. Base is $850,000 less $692,750, leaving $157,250 at 18.5 percent. Scaled is $1,500,000 less $1,125,000, leaving $375,000 at twenty-five percent. Conservative and Base retain one full-time owner plus three contractors; Scaled requires two full-time people plus four contractors. Do not multiply a single successful flip into an annual forecast without accounting for capital recycling, inventory duration, overhead, and failed investigations. Add the sixth-person structure only after completed-sale evidence and workload support it, not because a Day-90 sourcing threshold was reached. Track realized margin separately from modeled margin and explain every variance. The sprint succeeds when the next capital decision is better supported, even when that decision is to stop buying.
